title: Cookies! Cookies! Cookies!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and definition of cookies, starting with their chat about baking chocolate chip cookies at home. They discuss how cookies differ from cakes, breads, and pastries, and offer a working definition. The history covers Persian origins tied to sugar and spices, the Romans' twice-baked rusk and the etymology of biscotti and biscuits, the spread of cookies through the Crusades and Silk Road trade, medieval baker's guilds, early cookbooks like The Good Housewife's Jewel, and Scottish shortbread and its tax-evasion story. They cover American cookies including the Toll House chocolate chip cookie by Ruth Wakefield, the snickerdoodle and sugar cookie from Moravian immigrants, Moravian spice cookies, the New Mexico bizcochito, Amelia Simmons' American Cookery, whoopie pies, Oreos, Famous Amos, brownies as bar cookies, and cookie dough safety. The episode closes with a SketchFest announcement and a birthday shout-out.

segments.title: Opening banter and baking cookies
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with chit-chat about a dog, a wedding Josh officiated, and both baking cookies that night. They praise Sally's brown butter chocolate chip cookie recipe and discuss crispy versus chewy cookie preferences.

segments.title: Cookies versus cakes, breads, and pastries
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish cookies from cakes (dough versus batter, handheld and self-contained), from bread (no leavening in gingerbread or shortbread), and from pastries (pastries usually contain water). Chuck offers a definition of a cookie as a small, round, usually flat, handheld dessert made from at least flour, fat, and sugar.

segments.title: Sugar and cookie names around the world
segments.summary: The hosts note that sweeteners other than sugar exist but sugar is central, and that cookies have many names by country, including biscuits in England and Australia, galletas in Spain, and Plätzchen in Germany. The word cookie comes from the Dutch koekje, meaning small cake.

segments.title: Persian origins of cookies
segments.summary: Most food historians say cookies began in Persia around the seventh century CE, when sugar was available mainly to the wealthy. A popular story describes a Persian baker testing an oven with a bit of cake dough, though the hosts note that the story is not clearly true and ignores earlier evolution.

segments.title: Ancient precursors: honey pastries, rusk, and biscotti
segments.summary: Earlier precursors include Mediterranean honey pastries and Russian honey, rye, and berry cookies dating to the fourth century BC. The Romans made rusk, twice-baked bread that kept well as military rations. The word biscotti comes from Italian for twice baked, and biscuit derives from the same root.

segments.title: Spread via Crusades, Silk Road, and sugar's spread
segments.summary: Cookies and spices spread to Europe through conquest and trade, including the Crusades, which brought back ginger, cinnamon, cardamom, and sugar. Persia had access via the Silk Road, while Western Europe was far from it. Sugar remained a special-occasion good for much of Europe, which led to the tradition of baking cookies and sharing them at Christmas.

segments.title: Baker's guilds, home baking, and early cookbooks
segments.summary: Medieval baker's guilds tried to forbid home baking, but people ignored the rules and the enforcement faded over a century or two. Early cookbooks from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries included cookie and cake recipes, enabled by cheaper sugar from newly conquered sugar-growing regions. The Good Housewife's Jewel had vague recipes.

segments.title: Shortbread origins and the tax on biscuits
segments.summary: Shortbread from Scotland was a crumbly cookie made by swapping yeast for butter and adding sugar. The hosts say it was called bread to get around a tax on biscuits, according to a Scottish heritage site. They discuss the uncertain origin of the phrase 'that's how the cookie crumbles,' which Billy Wilder used in The Apartment.

segments.title: Macaroons, gingerbread, and Queen Elizabeth I
segments.summary: The hosts describe the European cookie boom from the fifteen to eighteenth centuries, including macaroons spreading from Italy to France and England. They discuss gingerbread, which appeared in medieval England, and the story that Queen Elizabeth I received shaped gingerbread cookies as tributes. They mention past Christmas episodes on gingerbread.

segments.title: American cookies: immigrants, pizzelle, teacakes, and early cookbooks
segments.summary: America's cookies reflect immigrant traditions, as shown by the pizzelle in the Midwest and the Scottish-derived teacake in the South. Amelia Simmons' American Cookery, the first American-printed cookbook, included cookie recipes with names like kinka woodles, tangle breech, plunkets, and cry babies.

segments.title: Moravian sugar cookies, spice cookies, and bizcochito
segments.summary: German Moravian immigrants in Pennsylvania and North Carolina are credited with the sugar cookie and the Moravian spice cookie. The sugar cookie was called Nazareth sugar cookies or Amish sugar cookies. New Mexico's state cookie, the bizcochito, was brought by Spanish colonists and co-developed by Pueblo people, and its name means little cakes.

segments.title: Toll House chocolate chip cookie and Nestle deal
segments.summary: The hosts credit Ruth Wakefield at the Toll House in Whitman, Massachusetts, around 1930 or 1931, with inventing the chocolate chip cookie by accident when she chopped semisweet chocolate in place of baker's chocolate. She struck a deal with Nestle for a lifetime of free chocolate and sold her rights, which Nestle held until 1983. They discuss chocolate chip variations and brownies versus cookies.

segments.title: Brownies, bar cookies, drop cookies, and icebox cookies
segments.summary: The hosts debate whether brownies are cookies, with Josh arguing they are bar cookies. They describe cut-out and drop cookies, and discuss the icebox cookie, a dough rolled into a log, chilled, and sliced. Fanny Farmer is credited with an early brownie recipe in 1905 and an oatmeal raisin cookie. The hosts also discuss the claim that a Maine housewife invented the brownie by mistake.

segments.title: Sandwich cookies, Oreos, Hydrox, and Famous Amos
segments.summary: The hosts discuss sandwich cookies, including Oreos, macarons, Ritz cookies, and the whoopie pie, which is linked to Amish workers. They note Oreo is the best-selling cookie, after knocking off Hydrox. Famous Amos was founded by Wally Amos, a former William Morris agent who gave cookies to clients.

segments.title: Cookie dough safety, Santa cookies, and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts discuss eating raw cookie dough, noting heat-treated flour as the safety measure, and Ben and Jerry's cookie dough ice cream. They close with the tradition of leaving cookies for Santa, dating to the Great Depression, and the hosts' call for listeners to bake cookies.

segments.title: SketchFest promotion and listener mail
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck promote SketchFest live shows on January 1 in San Francisco and mention a listener mail segment, followed by a birthday shout-out.

segments.title: Closing and New Year wishes
segments.summary: The hosts wish a happy birthday to Josh's wife and a happy new year to listeners, and give the email address for contacting the show.
